utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we continue, Mr. Mikulicic, the Chamber noticed that the Markac Defence has not joined in the good tradition to inform the public about the content of 92 ter statements by giving a summary. Could you please consider how to repair that and also to take into account that you are expected to prepare a summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, what will be your guidance as it refers to the previous witnesses that Markac Defence has been examined?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That you already prepare a summary and that we find a suitable time where, perhaps, some time remains where we can't fill the whole of the session and that you are then always prepared to read out the summary of other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Moric. I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we interrupted our discussions when we were discussing your position as assistant minister of the interior, during which time you witnessed the change of six ministers. Can you please explain to us the difference between the posts of an assistant minister and a deputy minister?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the Law on Internal Affairs and the decree on the internal structure and manner of work of the Ministry of the Interior, the assistant minister manages one of the sectors of the ministry; whereas, the deputy minister stands in for the minister in all the duties discharged by him; or, the duty -- the deputy minister has a very well-defined responsibility relating to a very specific -- or, rather, the assistant minister has a very specific responsibility for a given sector of the ministry; whereas the deputy minister stands in for the minister and acts on his behalf whenever there is reason for him to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the political parties which make up the government, what is the relation with -- what would the political relationship be with regard to the assistant minister and the deputy minister?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on how the government has been formed, whether it is a coalition government or a single-party government, the minister's membership of the political parties will be based on that. This, in a way, affected the position of ministers and deputy ministers on a government -- of a government. Sometimes it also reflected itself on the posts of assistant ministers in a given ministry. However, in the case of the Ministry of the Interior, at the time I was there as assistant minister, assistant ministers were prevalently appointed from the ranks of specialists and professionals and not along the political lines. Of course, there were exceptions to the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You were, thus, appointed assistant minister in the month of April of 1991. At the time, the Republic of Croatia was formerly part of the then Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. What was your main task when you were appointed assistant minister? Which particular field of activity of the Ministry of the Interior were you concerned with?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st of April, 1991, I was appointed assistant minister of the interior, who was supposed to manage the sector of ordinary general duty police. In other words, I was to deal with prevention. My basic task at the time was to organise the ordinary police force in accordance with the experience of democratic countries. Unfortunately, the events that followed considerably restricted my efforts to organise the police structure along those lines and not only -- not only restricted by also thwarted my efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up D527, please, page 2 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, I will show you now the decree on the internal structure of the Ministry of the Interior where, in Article 3, the way in which the ministry itself was organised is described. We can see that the Ministry of the Interior, according to the internal structure, is -- consists of the minister's office; the Service for the Protection of the Constitutional Order; and, under numbers 3 through to 10, various sectors. Under 3, we have the police sector. That was your domain of work, was it not?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I was in charge of the police sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The activities of the police sector are defined by the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And that's D1077 for the reference of Their Honours. Article 1, paragraph 2 of that law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly, what were the duties that the sector you ran, the police sector, were supposed to perform?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police sector was supposed to organise and then run the work of the ordinary uniformed police across the country. This means, initially, it was supposed to complete the transition that the police force was supposed to undergo, in view of the fact that a transition was taking place of a non-democratic society into a democratic society. Furthermore, the work of the ordinary police force was supposed to be organised in accordance with the specific geopolitical and geographic features of the country and set up the organic structures of the police that would be suited to the dramatic change that the Croatian society was going through, including the police. In that process, it was important to offset the internal difficulties we were faced with which were brought on by the transition process within the society and within the police force itself. A lack of understanding or a reluctance to accept the country's transition from a non-democratic to a democratic society and a lack of understanding for or a reluctance to accept the fact that the federal unit of a former federation was headed toward an independence and toward creating a state of its own, as well as the traumatic experience the police force was going through, such as terrorist attacks with fatal consequences, caused a great number of police officers who had been involved in the job at the time when Croatia was a federal unit to leave the ranks of the police force; and I'm referring to more than 2.500 officers who left the police force for all the aforementioned reasons. However, this was also caused by political pressure and the risk involved in the transition process for the police force itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When discussing this process where the former policemen were leaving the ranks of the police force, can this, in any way, be connected to any ethnic reasons?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, Croatia was still a federal unit, and, later on, as it acquired international personality, and still today it -- in its makeup, it reflects the ethnic composition. However, at the time when Croatia was a federal unit, the ethnic composition of the country was to the detriment of the majority Croat population. I'm stating this because it was a fact, and also to make the subsequent developments more easily understandable. The pressure brought on by the transition process and by the political and legal and traumatic police experience of the time out of the total number of persons who abandoned the police force, the majority were, truth be told, of Serb ethnic background, but not solely. I am convinced that that particular group of people included persons of all ethnic backgrounds in the Republic of Croatia, though the majority were of Serb ethnic background, since their number were, in the police force at the time, was disproportionately high.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In what way could that shortage of experienced policemen be compensated for, if at all, who left the police force at the time that Croatia was acquiring its independence?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two important reasons and a couple of other less important why this had to be done: The first reason was the intention for the Republic of Croatia as an independent and sovereign state to be organised in such a way that all its state mechanisms, including the police force, had citizens whose makeup would reflect the ethnic makeup of the country as a whole. The second reason was that we needed to equip ourselves in order to rise up to the challenge of stabilising security and the state of security which was deteriorating by the day. Accordingly, we organised courses at the police academy and other additional studies, through which we recruited citizens of the Republic of Croatia to the police force. However, recruiting policemen from the ranks of the citizens of the Republic of Croatia for the typical policing duties was a far lesser problem. A far greater problem was to compensate for the shortage of the police management personnel, a portion of whom had also left the Croatian police force. The period required for this shortage to be offset lasted much longer than the period needed for ordinary policemen to be recruited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, the witness earlier said that the -- there was a need to re-establish a balance because the Serbs were over-represented in the police force. Could you give us the numbers, how many, what was the percentage of Serbs in the police force; and prior to the movement where people abandoned the police force in relation to the Serb percentage of the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't say that it was necessary to establish a balance in relation to the ethnic makeup of the population. Rather, I said that it was only logical that among those who left the police force, the majority were Serbs, because they were -- their numbers were disproportionally high in relation to the makeup of the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, whether you call it logic or restoring a balance or changing the situation, my question was: What was the percentage of Serbs in the police force, and what was the percentage of Serbs overall in the population, before this change took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to the best of my recollection and knowledge of the data, before the outbreak of the conflict in the Republic of Croatia, there were 12 per cent of citizens of the Republic of Croatia of Serb ethnic background, and, on the police force of the then federal unit of the Republic of Croatia, more than 65 per cent were Serbs, or, rather, citizens of Serb ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. And after this abandoning the police force by many police officers, what -- well, let's say, on from -- the late 1995, how were the percentages then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1995, the percentage of citizens who were ethnic Serbs on the police force of the Republic of Croatia was some 4 to 5 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the percentage of the population of Serb ethnicity was how much?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To us, it always remained the same, Your Honours, because they were our nationals, regardless of what their temporary residence was; in other words, 12 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to the internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior and, particularly, to its sectors. You said that your sector was dealing with uniformed police, and all the other sectors had their own bosses, as it were; and they were also assistant ministers, were they not?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In principle, except for the office of the minister, every sector was headed by the chief of that sector. However, when it came to the actual running, day-to-day running, of every of the sectors, an assistant minister was appointed. In other words, chiefs of sectors were also heads of personnel; whereas, assistant ministers were responsible for the managing of the work of each of the sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, let's imagine this situation: An assistant minister for a certain sector had responsibilities for a different sector. For example, you were an assistant minister and you were in charge of the policing -- of the uniformed police sector. Did you have any authorities, and did you use your authorities over the sector of the crime police sector or special police sector? Was that -- was such a situation possible?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not common practice, and there was no objective need for any such thing. Not only was it not possible in former and legal terms, and it would not have been proper, but, in factual terms, there was no need for such practice. Every sector had its chief that was also the head of personnel, as I just described; and if the assistant minister was absent or was prevented from taking part in the daily management of the sector, then his role would have been taken over by the chief of sector. However, if there were special reasons, due to the specificity of a situation or a task, there was a person who was in a position to take over the responsible for the management of any of the sectors instead of the assistant minister, and that would be the deputy minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce Article 9 in the document that is on the screen. An Article which deals with the internal organisation of the police sector, Article 9, which is two pages after the one that we have on the screen at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Article 9 of the Decree on the Internal Organisation of the Ministry of Interior envisages the organisation of the police sector in the following way: There are departments which composed the sector, for example, the police department, the border police department, the traffic police department, the maritime and airport police department, the duty operations department, the explosion protection department, and, finally, the reserves department. Mr. Moric, how were the departments organised in view of the hierarchy system? Who was at the head of each of these departments?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the chief of each of the departments, and those chiefs were always appointed from the ranks of professionals with the longest possible professional experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: As we're looking at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- authorities of the police sector, we can notice that the -- it spans anything from the policing duties to the reserves' duties, border, traffic, maritime, airport duties, and so on and so forth. What kind of tasks are we talking about? What was their scope? What was -- what were the police supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned, at the very beginning of my testimony earlier this morning, specific geographical characteristics of Croatia, especially its very specific geopolitical position. These two positions, amongst other things, very much dictated the scope of the tasks that the police would not have had, or, rather, do not have in the countries which do not have such a specific geographical and particular geopolitical position. We will understand this best if we take the example of the border police. The Republic of Croatia, in view of its borders and their lengths, actually has a very low number of population. We have over 3.000 kilometres of state borders altogether which over 900 kilometres are maritime borders. We have, or, rather, we had, I apologise, while I was in office, we had 256 border crossings all together, and what I have in mind when I say that are border crossings for international traffic, interstate traffic, and border traffic; all the three categories are more involved. We also had seven airports at the time, and they were all international airports. All that time, including the time of combat activities, both offensive and defensives, were functioning without any interruptions. We had 19 maritime harbours for international traffic. Obviously, the geopolitical position of Croatia impacted the organisation and work of the police and particularly the border police, and even more so in cities close to the state border. Why was that? It is not possible to organise the work of the police in the same way when it comes to providing security and exercising control of the crossing of the state borders if that state border is with a neighbouring friendly state as compared to a neighbourly hostile state. In that context, the geopolitical position of our country imposed additional burden to the work of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In order to understand what you have just told to us, Mr. Moric, let's try to focus on the control of the state borders that the police exercised. You said that Croatia had about 3.000 kilometres of state borders --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber considers the level on detail on these matters not of assistance to it. No problem in saying that taking care of maritime ports, airports, and a long coast-line caused a lot of efforts; that's fine. But to know exactly whether it's 300 [sic] kilometres, how many airports there were, et cetera, is really not necessary for understanding, apparently, what you would like to elicit from this witness that it took quite a bit of work to deal with these matters. Would you please keep this in mind and be more focused in your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'll do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've described the tasks of the police and what the police had to do. However, if we go back to the year 1991, we will face the beginning of hostilities and the enemy activities which led to the war. How did the war start in the Republic of Croatia, and how did it impact the position of the police, and how did it reflect on the position of the police?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the transition from the legal state of a federal unit towards the international and legal subjectivity of an independent state, at that time, the Republic of Croatia did not have its own military. It had its police as the only legal and legally-founded organisation which was organised, armed, albeit with infantry weapons, but it was still armed. And that's why, on the one hand, there were great expectations on the part all citizens of the Republic of Croatia, the great expectations that they had from the police. But not only the citizens, but also the democratic authorities in the Republic of Croatia. And it was precisely because of that, because of the fact that the police was the only organisation that was legal and legally founded, the war started by attacks being launched against the police and then against the police stations. Police officers were attacked while performing their routine patrols while performing their routine tasks. They were ambushed. They were attacked during the night while performing their routine jobs. And later on, there were also attacks on police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce document D1088.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, I'm going to be show you a document that you yourself issued towards the end of 1991; to be more precise, on the 12th of December of that year. You sent that document to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia and to the Main Staff of the Croatian Army. In that document, you informed the Ministry of Defence about the number of police officers segregated by police administrations who were engaged in combat. The document goes on to mention those numbers, segregated by police administrations. And if we turn to page 2 in that document, we will see that, according to the document that you issued, a total of 3.000 police officers were engaged in combat, of whom 1.793 were active policemen, 921 were policemen in reserve, and 286 special police unit policemen. And they were all placed under the command of the Croatian Army. Mr. Moric, could you please explain the trend, or, rather, that situation in which police officers were placed under the command of the Croatian Army to fight for the country?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That situation that I have just described, which involved great expectations both on the part of the citizens and the authorities, for us, professional policemen, was extremely traumatic. Professional policemen everywhere in the world are educated to understand that the use of arms is their last resort. And they are duty-bound that before they pull a gun they have to estimate and assess whether there were any other means and any other ways to achieve the same goal. And only if they assess that there is nothing -- they can, only then, use a weapon but only gradually. First there has to be a warning, then there has to be a shot in the air, and so on and so forth. Here, as a result of the circumstances, we were put in a reverse situation, in a completely different situation. As we were defending ourselves, or as we were in -- in -- defending our infrastructure, primarily the police infrastructure and then the general infrastructure, the police officers were put in a situation to pull their gun immediately without any prior warning, and, thus, they became soldiers in a very informal which. So within that context, I believe that I should say to the Trial Chamber that over 350 police officers were killed; over 1500 were wounded. And many of them have become disabled as a result of that. When I left the system of the Ministry of Interior ten years ago, 98 policemen were still considered as missing and their lot was not known. Over 150 of them were taken prisoners. So those were the results of the factual situation that the police force found itself in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, in addition to combat tasks, the police still had to perform its regular policing duties, to control the border crossings, traffic, and so on and so forth. I'm not going ask whether that was difficult or not because I believe it's obviously. But I'm going to ask you: How did you organise yourselves in order to meet all the demands and requirements?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously the law, the constitution, and the legal system prescribes that the police have to perform their routine, typical policing duties. And, at that time, we were in a situation to have to follow rules; and, on other hand, we had to take part in the defence of the country. It was very difficult to reconcile the two demands. It was very difficult to meet all the expectations. However, we were in a situation that there was nobody else to do that. The police had to be involved in both, irrespective of the fact that it was both traumatic and difficult to organise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce 3D00766.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the time when the Croatian Army was being created and when the police had the role that you just described for us, there was also a need to create a special police units. What you see on the screen, Mr. Moric, is a letter, or a telegram, dated 19 July 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could the Court please produce the second page. And if we see that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You will see that you are the one who drafted this document. And you say that pursuant to the decision of the minister, the National Guard was being formed because a lot of police officers joined the police, -- the army. And in the third paragraph it says that units of should be formed from the ranks of the active police officers, whereby different administrations would form special police units. That was in mid-1991, Mr. Moric. Could you provide us with a context that provoked such an order and decision on the part of the minister?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the initial stages of the transition from a non-democratic into a democratic society in mid-1990 up until the date when the document was sent, the police had to deal with its routine policing duties and compensate for the shortages arising from the people leaving. It had to rise up to the challenges of organising the police force, since there were certain requirements that didn't need to be met by a federal unit but had to be met by a state. It was quite clear that the situation, as it was at the time, was untenable. For this reason, the parliament amended the Law on Internal Affairs, in order for it to provide for the setting up of the National Guards Corps, which retroactively can be seen to have been the beginning of the formation of the Croatian Army. As the conditions were met for the setting up of the National Guard Corps - Croatia did not have international personality at the time and was unable to have an army - men who were members of the reserve police force and some who were members of the professional police force and others who were members of the special police force, which wasn't very numerous at the time, joined the National Guard Corps in order to man it but also to man the special police force which was part of the police force I was in charge of. As part of this transition process, men who were members of the active and reserve police force joined the National Guards Corps, some joined the ranks of the special police force as well. Among them -- or, from their ranks, were people who gradually grew to become commanders of the first National Guards Corps units and, later on, the first units of the Croatian Army. As far as I remember, there were seven Generals, or there are seven Generals, who, at one time, used to be policeman. Among them is the former chief of the military police, who used to be a policeman. The former Chief of the Main Staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, the former defence minister, all of them used to be policeman. The current Chief of the Main Staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia was also a policemen at one time. The difficult process of internal transition again lay on the shoulders of the police force. However, the intention was to allow the professional police force to continue dealing with routine policing work; whereas, for the purposes of defence, which, by that time, it was clear to all was going to become an all-out aggression on the Republic of Croatia, separate units were to be set up that would take upon themselves the defence effort. In doing so, we were limited by the fact that the Republic of Croatia did not have an international legal personality at the time and was still regarded as a federal unit which was not entitled to its own armed force because there was, in existence, a joint armed force whose name at the time was the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can this document be assign add number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, the Chamber gains the impression that you have not understood the guidance I earlier gave. That is, to put focused questions without details. Even if the Chamber would not be aware of all the whys and the hows from what happened in 1990 and 1991, the Chamber feels that it still, with summary information on the background, could perform its function. Therefore, I again stress that you should focus on basic matters, because it's our impression that approximately 60 per cent of the -- if not more, of the information we received over the last hour was of hardly -- if at all, of any assistance. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we all due respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I think the historical context, especially as it regards to the role of the police, is very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We never heard that type of testimony during the entire trial. It is the position of the Markac Defence that this context is very, very important. I will stay within my estimated time in questioning this witness. And, Your Honour, I am almost finished with this topic and I will go to another topic. But, with all due respect, I simply stress that this part of testimony is of great importance for the Markac Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I was talking about the level of detail. If the Chamber would consider it totally without relevance, I would not have said what percentage was not of assistance. Then I would have said that nothing of it would have been of assistance. I said the basics of the background, fine, but not the level of detail in which you present it. And if you would be more active in intervening if the witness goes to tells us exactly how many Generals, ones that had been police officers or -- then if you keep better control of the examination, then we would certainly use our time in a better way. I think you asked -- the last thing you asked is whether the document could be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- admitted into evidence. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1843.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1843 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just for the reference of the Chamber, I could stress that the document D1084 is another order from that minister -- that time minister, Mr. Vekic, which deals with an organisation of the special police forces at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Moric, we have gone through the historic events which have determined the course of subsequent events in the Republic of Croatia, its international recognition, and the situation it eventually found itself in, as you recount in paragraph 7 of your May 2009 statement, where you say that the paramilitary and para-police forces of the so-called Krajina, with the help of the JNA, occupied almost a quarter of the territory. Mr. Moric, what became of the police units, police administrations, police stations which were located in what, at one point, became occupied territory?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even earlier on, and especially so once the area was blocked, the -- through what was known at the time as the Log Revolution at the time, these facilities were first exposed to attacks and then the personnel was driven out. The fact that the personnel was driven out meant that very little could be taken along. Whatever the policemen could carry of the office stationery and personal belongings they had, they took along. What remained of the inventory was destroyed, damaged, and finally seized. Whatever was not damaged of the infrastructure, it remained in the area. The personal was driven out to the free territory, the territory under our control; we took them in; and we organised them, initially, in order to ease their trauma; and subsequently to include them on the police force. The principle employed was that the police stations would be organised in such a way as to be physically as close as possible to the area they had been driven out of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your statement, and I'm staying with paragraph 7, you state that under the circumstances, the police work had to be organised in such a way as to allow, as smoothly and as quickly as possible, for the law to be enforced when conditions were met. And in this sense, operative action titled "Return" was put in place. Can you please explain to us what Operative Action Return was, what its purpose was, and how it was implemented in practice.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operative Action Return had two motivations: The first one was to organise ourselves so that we may be able to restore the police stations to their original locations as soon as may be, whilst expecting that the conflict would be resolved peacefully. The second objective of the operative action was to allow -- or, rather, to organise the police in such a way that would be suitable to the aspirations of the international community. Cyrus Vance was appointed the special envoy by the UN Secretary-General at the time, and he was the one who laid down the concept of a peaceful settlement to the conflict. The objective was to peacefully reintegrate this particular area into the legal and constitutional order of the Republic of Croatia. In this since, Mr. Vance envisaged what sort of police force would exist in the area, what sort of ethnic makeup it would have, as well as the scope of activity. In this sense, we organised Operative Action Return, and the minister appointed me as the person directly in charge, in order to envisage all the operative procedures, personnel procedures, and means and methods of providing logistical support, as well as professional and psychological support, required to ensure that the policemen were able to return to the occupied territory. Again, I repeat, in accordance with the concept of a peaceful reintegration, which my government had received by the UN special envoy, Mr. Cyrus Vance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can we set a time on this? When -- what was the date of the commencement of Operation Return?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless I'm mistaken, perhaps I should be shown a document to that effect, but I believe that it was the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, we will be skipping the period covering the developments within the occupied territory at the time when Croatia became recognised as an independent state and move on to mid-1995, the period shortly preceding Operation Storm, which, as the Trial Chamber is aware, started on the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And to that effect, can we please call up 3D00690.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, this is a document you issued on the 3rd of August. You will be seeing it on your screen presently. It's the 3rd of August, 1995, and in the top right-hand corner we can see that it says OA Return. And you sent it to all police administrations for the attention of the chiefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, it's an unusual time to take a break. It was not announced. But due to circumstances unforeseen, I would like to have a break immediately. And we'll then -- I apologise for this rather unexpected interruption. But I would like to have a break and resume at 20 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Moric, when answering my previous question, when discussing Operation Return, you said that you would like to be shown that document. We will do this shortly. But while we're still on this document, let's deal with it first. The date is the 3rd of August, 1995. You sent it to all police administrations, on the eve of Operation Storm, stating that measures should be taken immediately in order to supervise important facilities that are necessary for the defence of the country pursuant to government decisions which are in the respective police administration areas. Mr. Moric, can you tell us why did you send this letter to all the police administrations in Croatia on the eve of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this document was created, actually, what preceded it were four years of attempts to peacefully reintegrate the Krajina area into the constitutional order of Croatia. It was also preceded by many attempts of international envoys, and it came after a number of UN resolutions as well as two peace operations undertaken by the UN. The first one was called UNPROFOR, and the second UNCRO. Military -- a military liberation of the occupied territories was looming, and the Operation Return was envisaged. The police goals of that operation remained the same, although under different conditions of return which would no longer be by peaceful means and reintegration. In any case, once those areas were to be liberated, the police force was to go back to their respective police stations in the same personnel composition or in a composition close to that one, and in keeping with the constitutional law on the rights of ethnic minorities. They were supposed to exercise those duties in the newly liberated territories, hence, the name Operation Return. As for the need for this document, it was clear, based on the previous experiences, that we could expect terrorist attacks attempts in the liberated areas and in the area that was never occupied in Croatia. It was clear, from previous experience, that there would be attempts to stretch out our forces by means of terrorist attacks against vital infrastructure and facilities in the rest of Croatia. The government of Croatia, as in any other democratic sovereign country, decided upon a number of facilities which were important for the defence of the country. These facilities were the facilities including all types of infrastructure, such as road traffic, railway traffic, air traffic, electricity supply, water supply, hydro-electric plants, thermal plants, as well as energy facilities in general. This also included water supply and security infrastructure. That is why I issued this document in a timely fashion to caution the police administrations to act pursuant to their obligations under the law in order to undertake the necessary measures which had been planned beforehand to secure those facilities and to prevent any possible terrorist attacks against those facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moric, for this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1844.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1844 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Presiding Judge. Could we next see 1D610. This document initiates Operation Return, referred to by Mr. Moric. I did not put it on my list for examination-in-chief, but it was on the list of General Gotovina's Defence. In the meantime, with my learned friend Ms. Prashanthi, I agreed upon the use of this document; she agreed do it. I have a hard copy of this document as well, and I seek leave to provide the witness with it so that he could get his bearings on it in an easier way. And I had, beforehand, provided a similar hard copy to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, on the screen before you is a document dated the 30th of January, 1992, which basically launches Operation Return. You signed the document in the bottom right-hand-side corner. You sent it to the police administrations across the territory of Croatia. Therein, you explain that what was to follow was an overview of primary basic tasks of the Ministry of Interior in a possible UN peacekeeping operation. Towards the middle you say that the name of the operation was chosen for practical reasons, rather than a method of encryption, to cover anything for reasons of official secrecy. You then say that the police administrations, on whose territory there are no expelled stations or UNPA, UN Protected Areas, shall prepare for staff, professional, and materiel as well as technical assistance to other administrations. You forwarded copies of the constitutional law in question and the concept of the UN peace mission. Mr. Moric, when, in my previous question, you referred to Operation Return, you explained what the purpose of the operation was. And now we have the -- a chance to see the document itself. Did you have this document in mind when you referred to Operation Return, its temporal framework, and goals?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to thank the Chamber for allowing me to see the -- a copy of this document. This is, indeed, the document I had in mind. I wished to see it because I was concerned to see whether, as one of the attachments, there was a concept of the UN peace mission prepared by Mr. Cyrus Vance in 1991 attached to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, we won't go into any peace operation details, but for the needs of the transcript and to inform the Chamber, it would suffice, I believe, to just skim through the document to see what the obligations were that you pointed out to the police administrations for their action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For that purpose, I would kindly ask that, in Croatian, we see page 1D70-1102, and in the English, that is page 1D70-1128.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In item 1.1, you define MUP obligations as part of the UN peacekeeping operation in a way that would ensure that all staffing levels be reached in order to have all police stations and departments fully functioning. This is something you have already addressed, Mr. Moric; therefore, we can move to the next page, to item 1.2, whereby you order that accommodation and activating the expelled police stations should be taken care of. In item 1.3, you order that complete operative and forensic processing of all former policemen who committed crimes should be undertaken. In item 1.4, you order that complete operative and forensic processing of all citizens who have been indicated as perpetrators of crimes in temporarily occupied parts of the territory should be undertaken as well. These tasks, Mr. Moric, were motivated by what? What was the background to it?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The raison d'être of these tasks was the primary goal of this operative action. That is to say, to prepare ourselves for a peaceful reintegration of that area into the constitutional and legal framework of the Republic of Croatia, with the support of the UN peacekeeping operation, which is supposed to take place at the same time. The perpetrators of possible crimes should be excluded from that model if such perpetrators come from police circles or if they are Croatian citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let us go to the next page in the Croatian where we see an order to establish check-points on all types of roads leading into areas under the protection of the UN. These were actually types of border crossing, weren't they, Mr. Moric?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For practical purposes, one could say so; but formally and legally speaking, it is not. And even less so if we use political terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the area involved was not something that was disputed as belonging to the Republic of Croatia. It had been occupied and forcibly taken outside its constitutional framework. At that time, Croatia was still not an internationally recognised state, although its government did not recognise the authorities in the occupied territories. Perhaps a month after this, or -- sorry, I apologise. At about the same time, the international recognition of Croatia actually took place, turning Croatia into an internationally recognised entity. Therefore, we never consented to the use of the term "border crossings." But, for practical purposes, these were points at which people who were entering or leaving the area were checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation, Mr. Moric. Next, in item 1.6, it is stated that facilities need to be allocated for the accommodation of police monitors of the Blue Helmets, that is to say, the United Nations. What was the relationship of the police of the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia and UN personnel, as part of that -- of this project?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, from the police of the Republic of Croatia, saw the UN peace operation as a friendly attempt and assistance which would help us peacefully reintegrate the occupied territories into the legal and constitutional framework of Croatia. By the same token, we viewed the UN personnel involved as friendly. We believed it was our duty to help them in the performance of their tasks and their work but, also, to assist them in their daily routine situations, such as logistical supplies, accommodation, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the other hand, in the same paragraph, it is stated that the police monitors of the UN were there to put in place a double-layer security arrangement. That is to say, that the police was to undertake its duties without discrimination, and on the other hand, it was a guarantee to the police that it won't be exposed to attacks. Mr. Moric, in your understanding, does this accurately reflect the importance and the role of the presence of the UN police monitors?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, and as part of this concept of the peace operation, that was the general idea. In practice, unfortunately, it didn't quite work out that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we move to the next page, and if we look at item 1.7, we see that preparations for the establishment of a local police force are envisaged. Which local police force is referred to?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping with the concept of the peace operation, which, later on, was translated into the relevant resolutions of the Security Council of the UN but also in keeping with our constitutional law on the rights of ethnic communities and national minorities in the Republic of Croatia, which corresponded with the concept of the mission and the relevant resolutions of the Security Council concerning the UNPROFOR peace operation, what is referred to are the local police forces in the occupied territories of the Republic of Croatia at that time. The ethnic makeup of that force was to reflect the population makeup, and their authorities were supposed to be in harmony with the concept and, later on, with the relevant resolutions of the Security Council as well as with our constitutional law on the rights of ethnic communities and national minorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let's go to item 3.3 next, Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Croatian it is 1D70-1107; and in the English version it is 1D70-1132 and 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In item 3.3, mention is made of the need to assist the Blue Helmets in the demilitarisation of those areas which were protected by the UN. It is stated that: "After the withdrawal of the federal army and associated paramilitary groups, the disarmament of those who have not pulled out and gathering of discarded and hidden weapons, lethal assets, and equipment, shall ensue. Therefore, it is necessary to prepare a sufficient number of policemen for assisting the Blue Helmets in these tasks." Mr. Moric, can you briefly comment on the background of item 3.3?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a preparation -- or, rather, my request to police administration to get ready for the task at hand, the task that was envisaged by the concept of the peacekeeping mission and the relevant resolutions of the Security Council. Unfortunately, we have never been given an opportunity to carry out the task because the demilitarisation never happened. The federal troops never withdrew completely, and where they did, the military left their weapons and other military equipment and tools to paramilitary and para-police forces that were left behind in the area. In other words, the factual demilitarisation of that area never took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: To be perfectly clear, Mr. Moric, when you say "army" or "troops," what troops do you have in mind; what army do have you in mind?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term is federal, and the implication is the Yugoslav People's Army, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Under the following item, which is 3.4, there is a reference to site inspection and undertaking of other operative technical measures and actions with a view to document legally relevant facts about the crimes committed against humanity and international law and war crimes committed in UNPA areas and in other parts that had been or were still temporarily occupied. Mr. Moric, did the Croatian police ever manage to act in keeping with this obligation?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were faced with the fact that in these areas, at the time, we had numerous violations of international laws, numerous violations of the basic provisions of human rights and freedoms, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and within the context of the concept of the subsequently relevant resolutions issued by the Security Council about the peaceful resolution of the crisis, we knew from the police experience that such persons should be eliminated from such processes in order to facilitate the peacekeeping operation and, also, in view of the fact that they were the ones who had committed those grave crimes. In the police administrations, we had departments that were dealing with the elucidation of terrorist acts and war crimes. However, that task was never completed, at least not to the extent as it was envisaged. However, we are all encouraged by the fact that war crimes do not have the statute of limitations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Under 3.5, there is a reference to the establishment and the implementation of the function of the local police within the zones under the control of the United Nations or UNPA zones. Could you comment upon that task, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The organisation of the local police force, the authorities and powers of that police, were envisaged and laid out by the constitutional law on the rights of ethnical communities and national minorities in Croatia. That was part of our national legislation. It was also envisaged by the concept and the subsequent resolutions by the Security Council about the peacekeeping operations. From the international as well as national points of view, we sought a peaceful solution to the problem. And within that context, we wanted to organise a local police force in compliance with international standards. On the one hand, that are applicable to such cases, and on the other hand, in compliance with our own national laws. A mitigating factor was the fact that our own legal solutions and international standards very much corresponded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And, finally, Mr. Moric, let's look at page 8 in the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is 1D70-1109 in e-court, in the Croatian version; or 1D70-34 in the English version of the same text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: A reference is made in the second paragraph that the Ministry of the Interior wanted to carry out its tasks in a consistent way and that's why the ministry organised their Operation Return? The MUP personnel is hereby tasked to send all the correspondence and official documents arising from the UNPA peace operation to designate such documents as actions, and you are made responsible for the integral implementation of the action. Mr. Moric, we're going to see some other documents during your testimony. Some of them are marked by letters OA, which stands for the Operation Return. And tell us whether these markings have any other significance.

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, this is an accompanying letter to this document, and this document was sent to all the police administrations, and here I draw everybody's attention that the name of the operation arises from very practical terms, and it is not something that was intended to mask some tasks that should be considered a state secret. The name was devised for practical reasons. The code was known to the department in the ministry that was in charge -- in charge of following the tasks so that all the documents covering that action should -- could be grouped together; There was no other reason at all. And since I am answering this question, allow me to say also this: I would be very happy if we had been able to care out the Operative Action Return the way we had planned it. I would be happy if we had been able to achieve its goal, and the goal was peaceful reintegration of these areas into the constitutional and legal order. However, after four years of consistent attempts, we were still unable to achieve that goal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I think it is now the fifth or sixth time that you explain that all was planned in the context of a peaceful reintegration. That is understood by now. Whatever you say will be understood as being efforts made in this context. There is no need to repeat it again and again and again. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] could we please get the number for this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1845.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1845 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, let us go back to the times on the eve of the Operation Storm, or, rather, at its very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce D41.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You've already told us that the police were faced with some special tasks, tasks in connection with Operation Storm. I'm going to show you a document dated the 4th of August, 1995, the one that you yourself issued as part of the Operative Action Return. And you sent that document to all the police administrations to the attention of their chiefs. You say that the enemy is expected to try and launch sabotage actions in the liberated areas of Croatia, in order to instill disorder and the general feeling of unrest in those areas. And you order that the police should all immediately organise work in three shifts. Mr. Moric, please be kind and explain what did working three shifts mean when we're talking about a police organisation?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document containing this order was sent by myself to all the police administrations because I had had very clear indications that there would be attempts of terrorist acts. This was indicated to me by our secret services. And when we are talking about work in three shifts, in practical terms, that meant that there would be a lot more burden on all of our police officers who would be required to work longer hours in operations. To be more precise, the normal mode of work is in four shifts. The first shift is in the morning; the second shift is in the afternoon; the third shift is during the night hours; and the fourth shift is the one that had just finished their night shift is -- and is resting. Let's say we're talking about 1.000 police officers in every shift, this gives you a number of 4.000. When there is a requirement for all of them to work in three shifts, that means that they will no longer be working eight but, rather, 12 hours in every shift. Therefore, the first shift will be during the day; the second shift will be during the night; the third shift will be the one that has just completed their night shift; the fourth shift has been completely eliminated. And this has given us a surplus of a thousand police officers who could then be engaged on other tasks because they don't have to work in any shifts. But that means that everybody has to work longer hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Under item 3 of this order you issued, you asked for the security to be stepped up at the state borders, particularly in order to prevent illegal infiltration of groups or individuals, and bringing in weapons and explosives. Under number 4, you also ask for the stepping up of monitoring of vehicles and passengers. And under number 5, you ask for a stepping up of the services in all patrol and [indiscernible] duty sectors, particularly in places that you assess might be the object of terrorist attacks: bus and railroad stations, ferry terminals, and so on. If we turn to the next page in the Croatian version and look at item 6, we will see that you also requested that during alert, due do artillery or other attacks, citizens should be cautioned of danger of staying in the open area; and, at the same time, while they are in shelters, observation of residential buildings shops and other buildings of interest must be stepped up in order to prevent crimes such as theft, break-ins, and so on. Mr. Moric, could you just tell us briefly what motivated you to include item 6 in your order when you refer to the periods of alerts due to artillery or other attacks? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this document was created, we had already had four years of occupation behind us. Quite a huge area of Croatia had been occupied for four years, and there were daily artillery and mortar attacks and attacks from multi-rocket launchers from those areas, shelling 12 or even 14 towns in the vicinity of the separation line or the contact line. The town of Zupanja, for example, is a very specific example. For 506 days, that town was under constant alert. People spent all that time living in cellars, leaving the cellars only when they absolutely had to. So the meaning of this instruction under item 6 was as follows: When people had to spend some time in shelters during artillery attacks, on the one hand, they had to be cautioned to go there, to go to the shelters, because the experience had proved that some citizens had an increased level of tolerance, and although there was the sound of alert, they still did not obey measures that they should have applied in order to protect their own lives and the lives of their families. And, other hand, that while people were sheltered in cellars and other such premises, that the police should look after the protection of their properties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, even without the example, the Chamber would have understood approximately what was said here. You asked first what motivated the witness, what he meant by it, and then the obvious explanation came: You have to tell the civilian population to properly take care of themselves under those circumstances, which is, even without any further explanation, perfectly obvious from the text. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up 3D06-0965, please. Mr. President, this is a document which is not on our 65 ter list. But given the good cooperation we have with our learned friend, Mr. Waespi, I request that it be allowed to be included on 65 ter list so that we may present it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted to add it to the 65 ter list, as is leave granted to the previous document, where you said Ms. Mahindaratne agreed to have it in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, in fact, it was Mr. Waespi, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the previous time, I think, you -- this is the second time today that this happens. Well, I'll check that then. But leave is granted in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Moric, you said that, on the eve of Operation Storm, you were expecting terrorist actions to occur at the other end of the country in free territory. What I'm showing you now is a criminal report from the month of August 1995, where an unknown perpetrator is reported to have -- or, rather, who is reported to have been involved in an incident which was reported in the morning of the 7th of August, 1995, including a large amount of explosives that had been activated at the south-east side of the bearing wall of a bridge spanning the Bid Canal [phoen] on the 395th kilometre of the Zagreb-Lipovac highway. Now, Mr. Moric, this is one of the incidents that you expected to occur. Was this an isolated incident, or were there more such incidents taking place in that time-period?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, if I remember correctly, this was first in a series of terrorist attacks which occurred in the period between the 7th of August and sometime in the end of August. This attempt to blow up a bridge, which constitutes a segment of the Zagreb-Belgrade motorway, which continues on to southeastern Europe, was followed by two similar attacks on the railway line to the south-east of Slavonski Brod. This is the railway line between Zagreb, Belgrade, and southeastern Europe. The second terrorist attack on the railway line involved a detonation of explosives placed on the track, which blew up the train -- a train engine in the process. The other attack was thwarted because the 110 kilograms' worth of explosives were detected and neutralized.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry I'm interrupting you, Mr. Moric, now. But in accordance with His Honour's guidance, could you please focus on the facts without filling in all the details. You told us that this was merely an example that was to be followed by several other incidents. My question is as follows: To what extent did such examples of terrorist attacks on infrastructure in the free territory of the Republic of Croatia affect the work of the police?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a great extent, did they [as interpreted] have a bearing on the police work and not only on the work of the police but on the work of the other sectors of the Ministry of the Interior. This resulted in the attacks on the police. There was an attack in Rijeka where a suicide bomber careened a car into the police building in Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were so concerned about these attacks that, on this score, the minister of the interior --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Rijeka attack took place when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I remember, on the 20th of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were so deeply concerned over these terrorist attacks that, following the series of attacks I have just referred to, the minister of the interior called upon me to shoulder some of the burden and resign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be assigned a number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1846.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mahindaratne, could I inquire with you. Is there any dispute about these terrorist attacks which took place, from what I understand, the one on which -- which we see on the document far away from Sector South and the other one in Rijeka? Is there any dispute about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, therefore, half a word would have done that you could have agreed with Ms. Mahindaratne and then to say, without even showing the document, that there was a terrorist attack on the train bridge on that date. That was, in Rijeka, there was an attack such. And then you can ask the witness what caused this, and that is it that he would have to resign. That takes 45 seconds, and -- instead of going through all these documents. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up D583, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Despite the fact that you cautioned the police structures to heighten their alert because of the imminent terrorist attacks, they did ensue. But on the 8th of August, you sent another memo to police administrations where you state that despite the heightened measures, attacks were taking place. At the end of the document, you order that essential facilities and road infrastructures ought to be secured, and that facilities of importance to the state are to be also secured better, as did the infrastructure belonging to the police. How did this memo fit into the overall effort put in by the police to implement these heightened measures?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This meant that we had to step up our engagement in providing security to these facilities, including the facilities that were owned by us, on the one hand. And other hand, in view of the manner in which the terrorist attacks were carried out and the assets they involved, it was clear that they were directly linked and had a direct bearing on the liberation of the country. This, of course, added the pressure that had already been there for the police in carrying out their duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Next ensued Operation Storm. It was envisaged that police stations would have to be restored to the liberated area. As you said, they had already been on stand-by and in the proximity --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call up D465.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: -- because personnel had to be secured as well. This is your memo, dated the 3rd of August, 1995. We will be seeing it shortly. Mr. Moric, you, as assistant minister in charge of police, you sent an order to the police administrations, listed herein, that they should immediately proceed to gather personnel, 100 strong, in order to man these facilities. Now, what was the purpose behind this order, Mr. Moric?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would only like to first draw a distinction between separate police units of the uniformed police and the special police force. This isn't one and the same thing. What we are discussing here is the ordinary uniformed police. The request is that each of the police administrations listed here should place, at our disposal, 100 men who, depending on what the assessments of the developments would be, and depending on what the needs expressed by chiefs of police administrations would be, would be deployed to the liberated areas as assistance to the police stations that had been expelled earlier on and were about to return to the areas where they originally belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If we count them all together, we see that there are 16 police administrations, each was to provide 100 men, so it's 1600 men. And let's look at the date again; it's the 3rd of August. Or perhaps, rather than me telling the story, you should be the one telling us. Since this was ordered -- since this was then ordered that the police administrations received on the eve of Operation Storm, what sort of -- what is the character of the document in view of the time-line?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evidently, this is part of preparations. We will -- we have yet to see what is to come. This was not the final step when it comes to the efforts that we invested in relation to the liberated area. That's to say, the needs will arise for a more frequent rotation of men and for greater numbers of men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, where did all these men -- these policemen come from? You said that there had to be heightened supervision of all these facilities, calling for a greater numbers of men, and yet we -- you had to set aside what numbers of men for the territory covered by Operation Storm? How did the police structure cope with all these requirements?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was difficult. It depended on -- of course, it -- it had an adverse impact on the state of security for the police administrations that had to second these men to the liberated area. We expected the criminality rate to rise in the areas covered by these police administrations, but we decided to proceed this way, nevertheless, because we deemed that this damage would not outweigh the advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This document details the way in which manning was supposed to be carried out, and the penultimate paragraph contains your order, whereby the members of the separate police units to be deployed there had to wear a official police uniform, a summer shirt, berets, and boots. Now, Mr. Moric, what is the colour of the trousers and the summer shirt of the separate police units?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ordinary uniformed police has a blue uniform at all times. However, for situations that were not typical situations, grey colour could be used as well. However, the insignia on the grey background was always colour blue. That's to say, the coat of arms and the logo of the police always indicated, even where grey uniforms were concerned, that it was the ordinary uniformed police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let's turn to the second page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the third paragraph there, you order that the policemen had to ready themselves with the necessary gear and the hygiene kit that they normally had that would last them at least ten days. Can you explain this reference to what was to be at least a ten-day engagement of the policemen, in accordance with your memo? Did it have to do with the rotation of the forces or with something else?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My associates and myself, when preparing to help out the police stations, restore their authority in what was, by then, expected to be liberated territory, and expecting that the process of stabilising security in the area would not be a short one, but, rather, would be developed over time, in order to give an idea to the policemen who were preparing for this duty, we told them that they would be engaged for at least ten days. At the time we were conceiving this, we did expect the whole exercise to last some 10 to 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, Mr. Moric, police stations were set up in the newly liberated areas. This is something that has been established in this case. So the Knin police administration and the Knin police station were set up and became operational with the assistance of the separate police forces, as you put it just now. However, the Ministry of the Interior took another measure in this respect, and I will ask for your comments on this. This is the measure of dispatching a coordinator. Can you give us the context and the purpose behind this measure employed by the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. As the very title of the post in Croatian says, "coordinator," their role was to coordinate the work of police stations, to coordinate work among them, and to coordinate their work with police administrations. Their work was to be coordinated, and, under some specific serious situations, where the local police management had insufficient experience or had such experience for the first time. Given their background that they had in the ministry, they were supposed to help out the local police management in their day-to-day work. They were supposed to back their requests and decisions. Generally speaking, their role was to be of -- be professional and organisational support to the local police management.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of some of the coordinators that acted in the territory of the police administration of Knin, Mr. Moric?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were quite a number of them. I don't remember their names. I don't remember the names of the coordinators, but I remember the names of my two collaborators who coordinated or, rather, acted as their support. Their names were Mr. Tomurad and Mr. Franjo. I believe that, among the coordinators, were Mr. Baric, Mr. Buhin, and I apologise for not being able to remember the names of any of the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were the coordinators, sent to the field by the ministry, entrusted with some authorities to issue orders to the police stations in the areas which they were supposed to support?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, this would be directly in breach of the law, or, rather, the provisions of the Law on the Interior. The Law on the Interior provides that police stations, and police administrations as well, monitor the situation and occurrences in the areas where they exist, and they implement measures with a view to upholding law. In other words, the chiefs of the police stations, the chiefs of police administrations, all, in their respective, areas are the ones who implement the law; they undertake measures; they monitor a situation; and they take measures with a view to upholding the law. Or, in other words, the subordination structure starts with the chief of the police station, who is responsible to the chief of the police administrations. The chief of police administrations report to the assistant ministers for their respective sectors. And when it comes to the implementation of all the laws and tasks identified by the law, the chiefs of the police administrations report to the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce document P494.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, after the Operation Storm was carried out, the Croatian authorities managed to regain the territories that they had not controlled for four years. During that operation, there were various contacts with the population and members of the army -- the so-called Army of Serbian Krajina. Within that context, I'm showing you a document dated the 4th of August, also part of the Operation Return. You issued it, and you sent it to all the police administrations. And the subject of that document are collection centres. This document elaborates the organisation of collection centres, the reception of people, and so on and so forth. Could you please explain the context and motives which prompted you to sent this document to the police administrations?

utterances.speaker: JOSKO MORIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on previous experiences and cases when some parts of the occupied territories had been liberated, and particularly based on the most recent experience at the time of the liberation of Western Slavonia, it was very easy to foresee that we would be faced with a number of citizens of the Republic of Croatia who would lose direction, who would find it very difficult to decide what to do in the given circumstances, who would not be able to decide whether to stay on living in their houses or whether they would embark on a -- a journey together with other refugees.
